headline_en: Practising national unity and including expatriates
summary_en: Opinion piece by a Japan-based Bangladeshi community organiser arguing that the interim government has no expatriate representative and that expatriates' demands, such as voting from abroad and representation in parliament, are being ignored. He says the expatriate welfare adviser's first press conference offered nothing new, and proposes joint national civil-military exercises that include expatriates, especially in the cyber field.

facts.statement: During the 2024 mass uprising in Bangladesh, expatriates held protest rallies in streets and squares of many cities including Tokyo, and at one stage temporarily stopped sending remittances to express solidarity with the movement.
facts.source_in_article: Writer Sheikh Aleemuzzaman, Japan-based community organiser

facts.date: about one and a half months after the interim government was formed (August 2024)
facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul held his first press conference at the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment about one and a half months after the interim government was formed; the gist was keeping remittance flowing by increasing services and facilities for expatriates and expanding the international labour market.

The writer says the interim government has no representative of expatriates, and the expectations of 1.25 crore (sowa koti) expatriates, including the right to vote in national elections from abroad and to be represented in the national parliament, remain ignored; the reform road map includes no plan on this.

The writer objects to expatriates being treated as an exportable product for the international labour market and to the label 'remittance fighters' (remittance joddha), saying it does not reflect expatriates' core expectation of basic rights.

The writer proposes turning the army's winter outdoor exercise into a national exercise held twice a year (winter and monsoon) that includes students, the public and expatriates, with expatriates joining in the cyber field, which he says is very weak because of continued brain drain and weak infrastructure.

named_actors.name: Asif Nazrul
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Adviser in charge of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment; held first press conference about one and a half months after the interim government formed; writer found nothing new in it

named_actors.name: Sheikh Aleemuzzaman (শেখ আলীমুজ্জামান)
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Author; Japan-based expatriate community organiser

headline_en: Remittance of USD 42 crore came in five days
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 42.47 crore in remittances in the first 5 days of October 2024, with Islami Bank bringing the most. The article recaps September's USD 240 crore, the June 2024 record, the August exchange-rate band change and the shift from a boycott campaign to a campaign to send money legally.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the first 5 days of October 2024 was USD 42 crore 47 lakh, about BDT 5,696 crore in local currency.

In the first 5 days of October 2024, Islami Bank brought the most remittance (USD 10 crore 58 lakh), Janata Bank second (USD 5 crore 14 lakh), then BRAC Bank USD 3 crore 59 lakh, Mutual Trust Bank USD 3 crore 27 lakh and Agrani Bank USD 3 crore 13 lakh.
In the first 5 days of October 2024, state-owned banks brought USD 10 crore 80 lakh in remittance, specialised banks USD 1.5 crore and private banks USD 30 crore.
Remittance to Bangladesh in September 2024 was USD 240 crore, the second highest of 2024.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

After taking charge as Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024, Ahsan H Mansur met interim government Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus and it was decided to widen the band for interbank foreign-exchange transactions from 1 percent to 2.5 percent; under the crawling peg system banks can raise the mid-rate of the dollar from BDT 117 up to a maximum of BDT 120, so banks can pay somewhat more per dollar when buying remittances.

During the July-August 2024 student-public movement there was a campaign not to send remittance through legal channels; bankers say that has changed and many are now responding to a campaign to send remittance through banking channels.

named_actors.name: Ahsan H Mansur
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Took charge as Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024 (previously executive director of Policy Research Institute, PRI); widened the interbank foreign-exchange band from 1% to 2.5%

headline_en: Let this trend continue, let hundi stop
summary_en: Prothom Alo editorial welcoming the rise in remittances after the 5 August 2024 political change (USD 240 crore in September 2024, 80 percent above a year earlier). It calls for stronger action against illegal hundi, easier legal sending, more incentives and investment opportunities for expatriates, and describes how hundi rings lure expatriates with better rates.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in September 2024 was USD 2.40 billion (240 crore), against USD 222 crore in August 2024 and USD 133 crore in September 2023; expatriates sent 80 percent more than in the same month a year earlier.

After taking charge as Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024, Ahsan H Mansur met interim government Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus and it was decided to widen the band for interbank foreign-exchange transactions from 1 percent to 2.5 percent; under the crawling peg system banks can raise the mid-rate of the dollar from BDT 117 up to a maximum of BDT 120, so banks can pay somewhat more per dollar when buying remittances.

In the first two months of fiscal year 2024-25 total remittance to Bangladesh was USD 413 crore 79 lakh: USD 191 crore 37 lakh in July 2024 and USD 222 crore 41 lakh in August 2024. May 2024 was USD 225 crore and June 2024, the highest of the year, USD 254 crore.

Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur said at a Prothom Alo roundtable ('Where we want to see the banking sector') that the dollar price banks now pay for remittances is higher than the open-market (kerb) dollar price, and that this is stabilising the dollar market.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur

facts.statement: The editorial says several rings are active in various countries to grab expatriate Bangladeshis' money: they lure expatriates by saying they will get a better rate if they send money through them, take the expatriates' earnings abroad, and pay the money out in Bangladesh through their relatives and business partners (hundi), so the country is deprived of foreign currency.

The editorial calls for stronger drives against the illegal hundi business, making it easier for expatriates to send money through legal channels, more facilities and incentives for remitters, and free opportunity for expatriates to invest inside Bangladesh.
The editorial says the ceiling on investment in bonds designated for expatriates 'has already been lifted' and calls the earlier decision (to impose the ceiling) arbitrary.

named_actors.what_the_article_says: Took charge as Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024 (previously executive director of Policy Research Institute, PRI); widened the interbank foreign-exchange band from 1% to 2.5%

The article attributes the rise to the wider exchange-rate band introduced after the new governor took office and to the change from a boycott campaign to a campaign for sending through banks.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in September 2024 was USD 2.40 billion (240 crore), the second highest month of 2024; August 2024 was USD 222 crore and September 2023 was USD 133 crore, so growth was 80 percent year on year.
In the first two months of fiscal year 2024-25 total remittance was USD 413 crore 79 lakh: July 2024 USD 191 crore 37 lakh and August 2024 USD 222 crore 41 lakh. May 2024 was USD 225 crore.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

After taking charge as Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024, Ahsan H Mansur met interim government Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus and it was decided to widen the band for interbank foreign-exchange transactions from 1 percent to 2.5 percent; under the crawling peg system banks can raise the mid-rate of the dollar from BDT 117 up to a maximum of BDT 120, so banks can pay somewhat more per dollar when buying remittances.

The campaign during the July-August 2024 movement not to send remittance through legal channels has changed; bankers say many are now sending through banking channels in response to a campaign to remit legally.

headline_en: Remittance of USD 211 crore came in 28 days
summary_en: Bangladesh received over USD 211 crore in remittances in the first 28 days of September 2024, with weekly inflows falling in the second half of the month. The governor says banks now pay more for remittance dollars than the open market, and bank treasury officials say the bidding war for remittances has eased.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the first 28 days of September 2024 was over USD 211 crore.
Weekly remittance to Bangladesh in September 2024: first week USD 58 crore 45 lakh, second week USD 58 crore 26 lakh, third week USD 46 crore 70 lakh, fourth week USD 47 crore 88 lakh.
Remittance in the first two months of fiscal year 2024-25 was USD 413 crore 79 lakh: July 2024 USD 191 crore 37 lakh and August 2024 USD 222 crore 41 lakh.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 160 crore in August 2023 and USD 222 crore 41 lakh in August 2024, USD 62 crore more.

Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur said at a Prothom Alo roundtable that the dollar price banks now give for remittance is higher than the open-market dollar price, that this is happening for the first time, and that it is stabilising the dollar market.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H Mansur

facts.statement: Treasury officials of various banks said the competition to buy remittance by raising the price has eased, and the central bank's reduced strictness has created equal opportunity for all banks, so remittance has started to rise.

headline_en: Remittance of USD 116 crore came in the first 14 days of the month
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 116 crore 72 lakh in remittances in the first 14 days of September 2024, broken down by bank type. The article says remittance turned positive after the fall of the Awami League government on 5 August 2024, when expatriates switched from a boycott to a campaign to send more.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the first 14 days of September 2024 (to Saturday 14 September) was USD 116 crore 72 lakh: private banks USD 81 crore 69 lakh, state-owned banks USD 29 crore 72 lakh, specialised banks USD 4 crore 99 lakh and foreign banks USD 30 lakh.

Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 191 crore in July 2024 and USD 222 crore in August 2024; August 2023 was USD 160 crore. August 2024 was USD 31 crore above July 2024 and USD 62 crore above August 2023.

At one stage of the student-public movement many expatriate Bangladeshis announced they would not send remittance home; after the Awami League government fell on 5 August 2024 they began campaigning to send more than before, and remittance rose. Income came in higher in the first week of August even though internet and banking services were shut.

Between January and July 2024 the highest monthly remittance was June at USD 254 crore, the highest single month in three years (USD 259 crore came in July 2020); the second highest of the year so far was May at USD 225 crore.
Bank treasury officials said competition to buy remittances at higher prices has eased and reduced central bank strictness has created equal opportunity for all banks.

headline_en: Maximum dollar price for remittance is BDT 120
summary_en: Treasury heads of Bangladesh's state and private banks agreed at an online meeting on Thursday 29 August 2024 not to pay more than BDT 120 per dollar when buying remittances from foreign exchange houses. The aim was to stabilise the dollar price and end the exchange houses' monopoly-like hold, in which they held back remittances to get higher rates.

facts.statement: At an online meeting at 3 pm on Thursday 29 August 2024, attended by 42 treasury heads of state and private banks, all agreed that no bank in Bangladesh will pay more than BDT 120 per dollar when buying remittance from foreign exchange houses; those who did not attend were informed of the decision.
facts.source_in_article: Several bank treasury heads; BRAC Bank treasury head and DMD Md. Shaheen Iqbal

facts.statement: Banks collect remittances from foreign exchange houses and until now each bank bought at a different price; treasury heads say this let exchange houses build a kind of monopoly and hold back remittance collected from Bangladeshis abroad in the hope of a higher price, while some banks paid more to get more remittance.

The price at which banks sell dollars to customers has also been set at BDT 120, and on 28 August 2024 the dollar changed hands at BDT 120 in interbank transactions; if the treasury heads' decision takes effect the remittance and interbank dollar price will be the same.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Bank data / central bank report

facts.statement: After taking charge as Bangladesh Bank governor on 14 August 2024, Ahsan H Mansur met interim government Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus and it was decided to widen the band for interbank foreign-exchange transactions from 1 percent to 2.5 percent; under the crawling peg system banks can raise the mid-rate of the dollar from BDT 117 up to a maximum of BDT 120, so banks can pay somewhat more per dollar when buying remittances.
Remittance to Bangladesh from 1 to 28 August 2024 was USD 207 crore 10 lakh, against USD 143 crore 10 lakh in the same period of August 2023, USD 64 crore more.

headline_en: Remittance crossed USD 200 crore in 28 days of August
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh reached USD 207 crore 10 lakh by 28 August 2024, up USD 64 crore on the same period of 2023, after July 2024 had been the lowest month in 10 months. The article recounts the July bank and internet shutdowns, the change of government and the background of the foreign-exchange crisis.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh up to 28 August 2024 was USD 207 crore 10 lakh, against USD 143 crore 10 lakh in the same period of August 2023, USD 64 crore more.
Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 191 crore, the lowest in 10 months; the previous low was USD 133 crore 43 lakh in September 2023.

During the quota reform movement, banks in Bangladesh were closed from 19 to 23 July 2024 (government and general holidays), broadband internet was off for 5 consecutive days and mobile internet for 10 days, so foreign transactions with Bangladeshi banks almost stopped.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Bangladesh's foreign-exchange reserve once rose to USD 48 billion during the Covid pandemic, then fell quickly after the Russia-Ukraine war raised import costs while remittance and exports did not grow enough; the central bank has taken various steps to bring in remittances and other money from abroad.

headline_en: Remittance up 37 percent
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 153 crore in remittances in the first 20 days of August 2024, about 37 percent more than the same period of 2023. Bankers expect the month to end between USD 235 crore and USD 250 crore, helped by the wider exchange-rate band decided after the new governor took office.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the first 20 days of August 2024 was USD 153 crore, against USD 112 crore in the same period of 2023, an increase of USD 41 crore or about 37 percent.

In August 2024 remittance was arriving at an average of more than USD 7.5 crore per day; on 20 August 2024 alone about USD 11 crore came through banks. Bankers projected the month would exceed USD 235 crore and could approach or exceed USD 250 crore.
Between January and July 2024 the highest monthly remittance was June at USD 255 crore (this article's figure), the second highest May at USD 225 crore, and July was USD 191 crore.

Ahsan H Mansur, executive director of the Policy Research Institute (PRI), became the 13th governor of Bangladesh Bank on 14 August 2024; after meeting Chief Adviser Dr Muhammad Yunus it was decided to form a bank commission for banking reform and to widen the interbank foreign-exchange band from 1 percent to 2.5 percent, letting the crawling-peg mid-rate rise from BDT 117 to a maximum of BDT 120. Bankers say the decision was taken to encourage remittance through legal channels.

headline_en: High Court orders inquiry and report on irregularities in sending workers to Malaysia
summary_en: On Wednesday 21 August 2024 a High Court bench ordered the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC/Dudok) and the Bangladesh Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) to investigate allegations of irregularities, corruption and money laundering in sending workers to Malaysia and report within 90 days. The court also issued a rule asking why a full policy to ensure workers pay only the government-set cost of BDT 78,990 should not be ordered and why the more than 17,000 workers who could not travel in time should not be compensated.

facts.statement: On Wednesday 21 August 2024 a High Court bench of Justice Naima Haider and Justice Sashanka Shekhar Sarkar, after preliminary hearing of a writ, ordered the Anti-Corruption Commission (Dudok) and Bangladesh Bank's Financial Intelligence Unit (BFIU) to investigate allegations of irregularities, corruption and money laundering in the process of sending workers to Malaysia and submit a report to the court within 90 days.

The government-set cost for a worker to go to Malaysia is BDT 78,990; the High Court rule asks why a direction should not be given to make a complete policy to ensure payment of only this amount and stop excess fees being taken from workers.
facts.source_in_article: Petitioner's lawyer Md. Nazimuddin, describing the High Court rule

facts.statement: More than 17,000 workers who had completed all processes (including final clearance) could not go to Malaysia within the set deadline; the High Court rule asks why the recruiting agencies whose negligence and irregularities caused this should not be ordered to pay them compensation.
facts.source_in_article: Petitioner's lawyer Md. Nazimuddin; Prothom Alo report of June 2024 titled '17 thousand workers could not go to Malaysia even with final clearance'

facts.statement: The writ was filed on 15 July 2024 by S M Rafiq, proprietor of recruiting agency Messrs United Export Limited, attaching reports from Prothom Alo and other media.

The respondents, including the secretary for overseas employment, the foreign secretary, the commerce secretary and the ACC chairman, were told to reply to the rule within four weeks. Lawyers Md. Nazimuddin and Md. Abul Kashem Selim appeared for the petitioner and Deputy Attorney General Ainun Nahar Siddiqua for the state.

headline_en: July remittance lowest in 10 months
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 191 crore, the lowest in 10 months, after banks and internet were shut during the quota reform movement. Bangladesh Bank called in the heads of 12 leading banks and urged them to raise remittance even at a higher price, and the remittance dollar rate rose to BDT 120.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in July 2024 was about USD 191 crore, the lowest in 10 months; the previous low was USD 133 crore 43 lakh in September 2023.

Because of the situation around the students' quota reform movement, banks in Bangladesh were closed from 19 to 23 July 2024 (government and general holidays); broadband internet was off for 5 consecutive days and mobile internet for 10 days, so foreign transactions with the country's banks almost stopped.

In the first 3 weeks of July 2024 remittance came at an average of USD 40 to 50 crore (per week); USD 142 crore 93 lakh came from 1 to 20 July and USD 47 crore 97 lakh from 21 to 31 July, of which USD 12 crore came on 31 July alone.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Bangladesh Bank officials say that when someone sends remittance from abroad, banks are obliged to disburse it within 24 hours; but if the remittance houses in the sending country hold the money, it can take some time to arrive, though usually not more than two or three days.

As remittance fell, Bangladesh Bank called in the managing directors of the country's 12 leading banks and urged them to raise remittance; banks had been collecting remittance at BDT 117 to 118 per dollar and were advised to increase legal inflow even by paying somewhat more, and the remittance dollar price rose to BDT 120.

Bank sources say Bangladesh Bank has reduced its monitoring of dollar pricing and relaxed the rules on bringing any kind of money into the country through legal channels, which had a positive effect on remittance inflow in recent months.

In 2020, when international travel stopped because of the Covid pandemic, remittance through legal channels rose and monthly inflow averaged over USD 200 crore; total foreign-exchange reserves at one point exceeded USD 48 billion. After the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022 import costs rose and a dollar crisis appeared that has not ended.
By Bangladesh Bank's count, remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal year 2023-24.

key_quote_bn: কেউ বিদেশ থেকে প্রবাসী আয় দেশে পাঠিয়ে থাকলে ব্যাংকগুলো তা ২৪ ঘণ্টার মধ্যে বিতরণ করতে বাধ্য।

headline_en: Remittance inflow falls, only USD 13 crore 80 lakh came last week
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh fell sharply to USD 13 crore 80 lakh in the seven days from 21 to 27 July 2024, amid bank closures, internet shutdown and curfew during the quota reform movement. Bangladesh Bank urged a dozen top banks to bring remittances legally even at a higher price so that money does not shift to hundi, while expatriates were campaigning to leave banking channels.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the seven days from 21 to 27 July 2024 was only USD 13 crore 80 lakh. From 1 to 20 July USD 142 crore 93 lakh had come (USD 40-50 crore a week in the first three weeks), making USD 156 crore 74 lakh up to 27 July.
Another Bangladesh Bank source said remittance from 1 to 28 July 2024 was USD 165 crore 70 lakh.

The government imposed curfew from the night of Friday 19 July 2024; banks were closed from 19 to 23 July (until Tuesday) and online transactions stopped as there was no internet (broadband off 5 days, mobile internet 10 days). Banks reopened on 24 July after five days without transactions; that day the SWIFT system was disconnected so no remittance money came to many banks, and normal global transactions resumed the next day.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Bangladesh Bank officials say that when someone sends remittance from abroad, banks are obliged to disburse it within 24 hours; but if the remittance houses in the sending country hold the money, it can take some time to arrive, though usually not more than two or three days.

The managing directors of a dozen top banks were called in and urged to raise remittance; banks had been collecting remittance at BDT 117-118 per dollar and were told to bring it through legal channels even at a somewhat higher price and to watch that remittance does not shift to hundi because of the lower dollar price.

A bank managing director, speaking anonymously, said the central bank promised not to impose strictness over paying higher prices, that banks were desperately booking dollars with remittance houses, and that many expatriates had begun a campaign to move outside banking channels.
facts.source_in_article: Unnamed managing director of a bank

facts.statement: Bank sources say Bangladesh Bank has reduced its monitoring of dollar pricing and relaxed the rules on bringing any kind of money into the country through legal channels, which had a positive effect on remittance inflow in recent months.

In 2020, when international travel stopped because of the Covid pandemic, remittance through legal channels rose and monthly inflow averaged over USD 200 crore; total foreign-exchange reserves at one point exceeded USD 48 billion. After the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022 import costs rose and a dollar crisis appeared that has not ended. (Bankers' view that the crisis has not ended.)
By Bangladesh Bank's count, remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal year 2023-24.

headline_en: Even six days did not bring one day's worth of remittance
summary_en: From 19 to 24 July 2024 Bangladesh received only USD 7 crore 80 lakh in remittances, about what had been arriving per day in the first 18 days of the month. Banks were shut and internet was off during the curfew, and money sent during the closure had not been credited on the first reopening day as expected.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in the six days from 19 to 24 July 2024 was USD 7 crore 80 lakh, whereas in the first 18 days of July 2024 it averaged USD 7 crore 90 lakh per day.

Banking operated on only one day between 19 and 24 July 2024: curfew began on the night of Friday 19 July, banks were closed until Tuesday (23 July) and online transactions were off without internet; banks reopened on 24 July with transactions for four hours from 11 am to 3 pm. Remittance could not come through banks from 19 to 23 July, and money sent in that period was supposed to be credited on the first reopening day (Wednesday 24 July) but was not.

Bangladesh Bank officials say banks are obliged to disburse remittance within 24 hours of it being sent from abroad, but if remittance houses in the sending country hold the money it can take some time to arrive.

Remittance through legal channels from 1 to 24 July was USD 158 crore 60 lakh in 2023 and USD 150 crore in 2024; of the 2024 figure USD 142 crore 20 lakh came in the first 18 days and USD 7 crore 80 lakh from 19 to 24 July.
Remittance from 1 to 18 July was USD 129 crore 70 lakh in 2023 and USD 142 crore 20 lakh in 2024, a big jump before the shutdown.
Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore, the highest for a single month in three years; before that USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Mutual Trust Bank managing director Syed Mahbubur Rahman said Bangladesh's financial transactions with the world were cut off for five days because the internet was off, so remittance could not come; money sent in that period should have arrived on Wednesday or Thursday, otherwise on the coming Sunday or Monday, and if it does not come in those two days it means remittance has taken a blow.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director, Mutual Trust Bank

facts.statement: Bank sources say Bangladesh Bank has reduced its monitoring of dollar pricing and relaxed the rules on bringing any kind of money into the country through legal channels, which had a positive effect on remittance inflow in recent months.

In 2020, when international travel stopped because of the Covid pandemic, remittance through legal channels rose and monthly inflow averaged over USD 200 crore; total foreign-exchange reserves at one point exceeded USD 48 billion. After the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022 import costs rose and a dollar crisis appeared that has not ended.
By Bangladesh Bank's count, remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal year 2023-24.

headline_en: USD 254 crore remittance in June, highest in three years
summary_en: Expatriates sent USD 254 crore 20 lakh to Bangladesh in June 2024, the month of Eid al-Adha, the highest single month in three years. Bankers link the rise to the higher dollar rate after the May 2024 crawling peg (BDT 117 official, BDT 118-119 actually paid), relaxed rules, and possibly previously laundered money returning as remittance.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in June 2024 was USD 254 crore 20 lakh, the highest single month in three years (USD 259 crore came in July 2020); June 2023 was USD 219 crore 90 lakh.
Within June 2024, USD 146 crore came in the first 12 days, USD 205 crore 20 lakh up to 23 June, and USD 16 crore 70 lakh in the three days 28 to 30 June.

Discussion in the banking sector about the sudden jump: some say money laundered abroad earlier is being brought back as remittance; others say expatriates are encouraged to use formal channels because banks now pay a high dollar rate for remittance.

Bank sources say Bangladesh Bank has reduced its monitoring of dollar pricing and relaxed the rules on bringing any kind of money into the country through legal channels, which had a positive effect on remittance inflow in recent months.
Expatriates usually send more remittance to relatives at Eid than in other months; Eid al-Adha was celebrated in Bangladesh on 17 June 2024.

Remittance in May 2024 was USD 225 crore. Bank officials say legal remittance started rising after Bangladesh Bank raised the dollar rate by BDT 7 in one jump to BDT 117 in May 2024; although the rate on paper is BDT 117, banks bought remittance dollars at BDT 118 to 119, and the bank that pays more gets more dollars from expatriates.

Bangladesh's foreign-exchange reserve rose to USD 2,715 crore at the end of June 2024, helped by the central bank buying dollars from local banks and by loans and budget support from development partners that arrived in the last week of June.

In 2020, when international travel stopped because of the Covid pandemic, remittance through legal channels rose and monthly inflow averaged over USD 200 crore; total foreign-exchange reserves at one point exceeded USD 48 billion. After the Russia-Ukraine war began in February 2022 import costs rose and a dollar crisis appeared that has not ended.
By Bangladesh Bank's count, remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 2,391 crore in fiscal year 2023-24.

headline_en: USD 146 crore remittance came in the first 12 days of the month
summary_en: Ahead of Eid al-Adha, expatriate Bangladeshis sent USD 146 crore through banks in the first 12 days of June 2024, about 74 percent more than the same period of 2023. Bankers link the rise to Bangladesh Bank raising the dollar rate by BDT 7 to BDT 117 in May 2024.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh through banks from 1 to 12 June 2024 was USD 146 crore, against USD 84 crore in the same period of June 2023, an increase of USD 62 crore or about 74 percent.

Remittance in May 2024 was USD 225 crore, the highest in 46 months, an average of USD 7 crore 25 lakh per day; in the first 12 days of June 2024 the daily average was USD 12 crore 17 lakh, about USD 5 crore a day more.

Expatriate Bangladeshis send more remittance to relatives before Eid than in other months; Eid al-Adha was on Monday 17 June 2024. Banking-sector people expected June 2024 remittance to exceed USD 250 crore if the trend continued.
Banking-sector people say remittance through legal channels rose after Bangladesh Bank raised the dollar price by BDT 7 in one jump to BDT 117 in May 2024.
Remittance to Bangladesh in fiscal year 2022-23 was USD 2,161 crore; in the first 11 months of fiscal year 2023-24 (printed as 'July-June') it was USD 2,137 crore.

headline_en: 4 workers kidnapped in Libya rescued, relief for families
summary_en: Four Bangladeshi workers from Charbiaghat village in Gurudaspur upazila, Natore, who had been kidnapped in Libya and tortured for ransom, were rescued by the Libyan army in an operation at about 9 am local time on Sunday 9 June 2024 and are in Libyan police custody. The kidnappers, whom the victims said were Bangladeshi, had sent torture videos and demanded BDT 10 lakh each; none were caught.

facts.statement: Four kidnapped Bangladeshi workers were rescued by the Libyan army in an operation at about 9 am local time on Sunday 9 June 2024; they are in the custody of Libyan police, and the kidnappers could not be detained.
facts.source_in_article: Gurudaspur police station OC Ujjal Hossain; Natore SP Tariqul Islam

facts.statement: Kidnappers in Libya sent videos of the four workers being tortured to their relatives' mobile phones and demanded BDT 10 lakh ransom each; the video and demand were sent to the families on 2 June 2024, and the men had been tortured for more than a week after the kidnapping.
The four victims told their families that the kidnappers in Libya were Bangladeshi.

According to the families, the four workers (Sohan Pramanik 20, Sagar Hossain 24, Nazim Ali 36, Bidyut Hossain 26, all of Charbiaghat village, Gurudaspur, Natore) went to Libya two years before June 2024.

Natore Superintendent of Police Tariqul Islam confirmed the rescue at about 12 noon on 9 June 2024, and on his instruction the Gurudaspur police station officer-in-charge informed the workers' families.

Nazim Ali's wife Nadira Begum said the family borrowed money to send her husband to Libya, leaving two small children at home (amount not stated). Sohan Pramanik's mother Duli Khatun said the family had been preparing to raise the ransom money before the rescue.

headline_en: Stop the brokers' dominance in Mymensingh
summary_en: Prothom Alo editorial on broker rings at the Mymensingh Regional Passport Office. It says flawed applications are accepted if the applicant gets a code number by paying extra at a computer shop near the office, while correct applications are rejected on pretexts so people are forced to use brokers, and that insiders in the office must be involved.

facts.statement: When a passport application form has missing information or the applicant forgets supporting papers such as copies of the national ID card or birth registration certificate, the passport office does not accept the application and tells the person to come back with it properly filled in and with all required documents.

At the Mymensingh Regional Passport Office, a flawed application becomes acceptable if the applicant obtains a code number by paying extra money or a bribe at a computer shop near the passport office; the application is accepted on sight of the shop's code without verification, even where the address is not right or the nationality or character certificate is doubtful.

Many passport applicants at Mymensingh complain that even when everything in their application is correct it is refused on some pretext of a defect, forcing them to go to a broker, which costs them extra money and hardship.
facts.source_in_article: Passport applicants' complaints cited in editorial

facts.statement: The editorial says brokers used to hang around inside the passport office; after regular drives they changed their method (working through nearby computer shops), and that drives cannot stop them unless those inside the office are removed. It warns the ring makes it possible for non-citizens or Rohingya to get passports.

headline_en: USD 214 crore remittance came in May, growth 38 percent
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh through legal channels was USD 214 crore from 1 to 29 May 2024, about 38 percent above the same period of 2023. Banking-sector people attribute the rise to the crawling peg introduced on 8 May 2024, which lifted the dollar rate from BDT 110 to a mid-rate of BDT 117.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh through legal channels from 1 to 29 May 2024 was USD 214 crore, against USD 155 crore in the same period of 2023, an increase of USD 59 crore or about 38 percent; April 2024 was USD 204 crore, so two consecutive months were above USD 200 crore.

On 8 May 2024 Bangladesh Bank introduced the crawling peg method for setting the dollar exchange rate, fixing a mid-rate of BDT 117 and telling banks to trade freely around it; before that the fixed price in the banking sector was BDT 110 per dollar, so the dollar price rose BDT 7 in one jump.
Banking-sector people believe expatriates increased sending through banks because they now get a good dollar price through legal channels.

The May 2024 figure is up to Wednesday 29 May; with Thursday 30 May added, the final May figure was expected to exceed USD 220 crore, which would be the highest single month of fiscal year 2023-24. The highest in July-April of that fiscal year was February 2024 at USD 216 crore.
Total remittance from July 2023 to 29 May 2024 was USD 2,126 crore, against USD 1,927 crore in the same period of fiscal year 2022-23, an increase of USD 199 crore or about 10.5 percent.

headline_en: Bank security guard took returnee migrant workers' money by deception, later returned some
summary_en: At the Akkelpur branch of Rupali Bank in Joypurhat, security guard Shahidul Islam took a cut of the BDT 13,500 incentive paid to each of 17 returnee migrant workers by opening their accounts, keeping their chequebooks with three signed cheques, withdrawing the full amount and giving them BDT 8,000 each. On Monday 20 May 2024 the workers protested; with the mayor present he returned BDT 3,000 each to four of them and promised to repay the others.

facts.statement: At Rupali Bank's Akkelpur branch (Joypurhat), security guard Shahidul Islam opened Rupali Bank accounts for 17 returnee migrant workers, kept each one's whole chequebook including three signed cheque leaves, and after the incentive money was credited used the signed cheques to withdraw the full BDT 13,500 incentive, giving each worker BDT 8,000.
The incentive money for returnee migrant workers credited to the bank accounts in this case was BDT 13,500 per person (the article does not name the scheme or the paying body).

On Monday 20 May 2024 the cheated returnees went to the branch to demand the rest; after an argument, and after they complained to the branch manager and then to the UNO, the guard returned BDT 3,000 each to four returnees at 4 pm in the presence of Akkelpur municipality mayor Shahidul Alam Chowdhury and promised to repay the others the same way.

The victims said about 20 days earlier the guard called 5 to 6 of them to the bank and handed over BDT 8,000 each, promising the rest on 20 May; on 20 May he misbehaved with them, they refused a BDT 3,000 settlement mediated by College Bazar traders' association president Kazi Shafiuddin, and then went to the UNO.

Akkelpur UNO Monjurul Alam said the returnees complained orally that they had been paid less by trickery; he told them to submit a written complaint and spoke to the Rupali Bank branch manager, after which the returnees did not come back to him. The guard said 'I have settled it'. No case or disciplinary action is reported.

headline_en: 21% of migrants entering Europe via the Mediterranean are Bangladeshi
summary_en: IOM Director General Amy Pope, visiting Dhaka, said on Tuesday 7 May 2024 that Bangladeshis top the list of people reaching Europe across the Mediterranean in the first four months of 2024: 3,425 of 16,200 arrivals, or 21 percent. She said 283 Bangladeshis have died on the route since 2014 and that traffickers use social media skilfully while information on legal routes and required skills is under-funded.

facts.statement: From January to 30 April 2024, 16,200 nationals of various countries reached Europe across the Mediterranean, of whom 3,425 were Bangladeshi (21 percent), putting Bangladesh at the top of the list.
In 2023 Bangladeshis were fourth on the list of irregular migration across the Mediterranean.
In 2023, 5,000 migrants died (worldwide); 524 of them died in the Mediterranean, on the route Bangladeshis usually take to Italy.
Since 2014, 283 Bangladeshis have died on the way to Europe across the Mediterranean.

Migration from Bangladesh to Europe via the Middle East is increasing; Amy Pope said many of these migrants were working in the Middle East, and that the tendency to cross to Europe via the Mediterranean has increased since 2015.
facts.source_in_article: IOM Director General Amy Pope; reporter's question

facts.statement: Amy Pope said human traffickers use social media in a sophisticated way, taking account of the situation worldwide.

Amy Pope said there are not enough legal pathways for would-be migrants, not enough is invested in informing people about legal ways to migrate, and people cannot properly learn what skills they need for legal migration and how to get them; to counter traffickers on social and digital media people must be properly informed about legal migration routes.

IOM's global report for 2024 says about 15 lakh people have been displaced in Bangladesh; Amy Pope said data and research are needed to understand whether large numbers are migrating because of climate change.
facts.source_in_article: IOM World Migration Report 2024; Amy Pope

headline_en: Remittance worldwide has grown 650 percent
summary_en: IOM's World Migration Report 2024, released in Dhaka on Tuesday 7 May 2024, says global remittances rose from USD 128 billion in 2000 to USD 831 billion in 2022, a 650 percent increase. The article gives global migrant and displacement numbers and remarks by IOM Director General Amy Pope and Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud; it has no Bangladesh-specific migration data beyond Rohingya figures.

facts.statement: Global remittance was USD 128 billion in 2000 and USD 831 billion in 2022, a 650 percent increase; of the 2022 total, USD 647 billion went to low- and middle-income countries, more than their foreign development aid and foreign investment.
facts.source_in_article: IOM World Migration Report 2024; IOM Director General Amy Pope

facts.statement: By 2020 statistics there were about 28 crore 10 lakh migrants worldwide: 14 crore 60 lakh men and 13 crore 50 lakh women, with 2 crore 80 lakh child migrants; by 2019 figures there were 16 crore 90 lakh labour migrants.
facts.source_in_article: IOM Director General Amy Pope presenting the report

facts.statement: The number of people displaced by conflict, violence, disaster and other causes is 11 crore 70 lakh, of whom 7 crore 12 lakh are internally displaced and 3 crore 53 lakh are refugees, the highest ever.

The biennial World Migration Report, published since 2000, was launched for the first time outside IOM headquarters in Geneva, in Dhaka on 7 May 2024; Amy Pope cited Bangladesh's role as a champion country of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration.
Foreign Minister Hasan Mahmud said repatriating the 13 lakh Rohingya sheltering in Bangladesh is a huge challenge.

headline_en: Remittance suddenly rose on the last day of April
summary_en: Remittance of USD 13 crore 50 lakh arrived on the last day of April 2024, taking the month to USD 204 crore 30 lakh, 21 percent above April 2023. Bankers say Bangladesh Bank let banks buy remittance at up to BDT 117 per dollar, which with the 5 percent total incentive makes about BDT 123, and that end-of-month account updating also played a part.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in April 2024 was USD 204 crore 30 lakh, 21 percent more than April 2023; USD 13 crore 50 lakh came on the last day (30 April), about double the roughly USD 6.5 crore daily average of the first 29 days.
Remittance was USD 128 crore 15 lakh in the first 19 days of April 2024 and, as printed, '190 crore 80 dollars' in the first 29 days.

A senior official of one bank said that because remittance was below expectation early in April 2024, Bangladesh Bank allowed banks to buy remittance at up to BDT 117 per dollar and many banks bought remittance dollars at the last moment.
If a remittance dollar is bought at BDT 117, with the total 5 percent incentive given by the government and the bank the value of the dollar comes to about BDT 123.

A bank managing director said remittance that arrives earlier is sometimes not added to the accounts for various reasons and accounts are updated at month end, which can also raise the last day's figure.
Eid al-Fitr was in April 2024, but unlike most years no extra Eid surge in remittance was seen, bankers said.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 210 crore in January 2024, USD 216 crore 60 lakh in February 2024 and USD 199 crore 68 lakh in March 2024.

Most banks were buying remittance at BDT 116.50 to BDT 117 per dollar and some crisis-hit banks at higher prices, although the official dollar rate was BDT 110; overall inflation was still above 9 percent.

headline_en: USD 190 crore remittance in 29 days of April
summary_en: Bangladesh received about USD 190 crore in remittances through banking channels in the first 29 days of April 2024, with no extra Eid al-Fitr surge. Most banks were buying remittance dollars at BDT 115-116 against an official rate of BDT 110.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh through banking channels in the first 29 days of April 2024 was, as printed, '190 crore 80 dollars'; USD 128 crore 15 lakh came in the first 19 days and USD 62 crore 65 lakh in the next 10 days, an average of USD 6 crore a day.
Eid al-Fitr was celebrated in April 2024, but bankers saw no extra Eid-related surge in remittance, unlike most years.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 210 crore in January 2024, USD 216 crore 60 lakh in February 2024 and USD 199 crore 68 lakh in March 2024.
Most banks were buying remittance at BDT 115 to 116 per dollar and some crisis-hit banks at higher prices, although the official dollar price was BDT 110.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore 7 lakh in fiscal year 2022-23, USD 2,103 crore 17 lakh in 2021-22 and USD 2,477 crore 77 lakh in 2020-21, the highest for any fiscal year so far.

key_quote_bn: বেশির ভাগ ব্যাংক এখন ১১৫ থেকে ১১৬ টাকা দরে প্রবাসী আয় কিনছে।

headline_en: Dhaka tops remittance receipts, followed by Chattogram, Sylhet, Cumilla and Noakhali
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's district-wise report for July 2023 to February 2024 shows most remittance arrives at bank branches in Dhaka district, followed by Chattogram, Sylhet, Cumilla and Noakhali. Bank officials say migrant-heavy districts receive less than expected because many expatriates have settled abroad and are selling assets at home and taking the money out.

facts.statement: District-wise remittance received in July 2023 - February 2024: Dhaka USD 523 crore, Chattogram USD 142 crore, Sylhet USD 87 crore, Cumilla USD 81 crore, Noakhali USD 46 crore, Brahmanbaria USD 38 crore, Feni USD 37 crore, Moulvibazar USD 36 crore, Chandpur USD 35 crore and Narsingdi USD 25 crore.
Expatriates sent USD 1,507 crore to Bangladesh in the eight months July 2023 - February 2024, including USD 216 crore 46 lakh in February 2024 and USD 210 crore in January 2024.

Bank officials say migrant-heavy districts should be receiving more than they do, but many expatriates have settled permanently abroad and are instead selling assets in Bangladesh and taking the money abroad, increasing money laundering.

Calendar-year remittance to Bangladesh: USD 2,190 crore in 2023, USD 2,130 crore in 2022 (growth about 3 percent in 2023), USD 2,207 crore in 2021, USD 2,173 crore in 2020 and USD 1,833 crore in 2019. December 2023 was USD 198 crore 98 lakh and November 2023 USD 193 crore.

The official dollar price for buying remittance was BDT 110, but banks were buying at higher prices because of the dollar crisis, which is raising legal remittance; bank officials also think some people are bringing back laundered money by showing it as remittance.

The Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers Association (BAFEDA) and the Association of Bankers Bangladesh (ABB), both bodies of commercial banks, have been setting the dollar exchange rate from time to time depending on supply and demand.
Banks in Bangladesh now give their own incentive on remittances equal to the government's 2.5 percent incentive (so 2.5 percent from government plus 2.5 percent from the bank).

key_quote_bn: ব্যাংকগুলো অবশ্য এখন সরকারের আড়াই শতাংশ প্রণোদনার পাশাপাশি নিজেরাও সমপরিমাণ প্রণোদনা দিচ্ছে।

headline_en: Remittance picks up before Eid, USD 46 crore in five days
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh picked up before Eid al-Fitr, with about USD 45 crore 54 lakh arriving through banking channels in the first five days of April 2024, after a weaker March. The article gives the split by bank type and recent monthly and yearly totals.

facts.statement: About USD 45 crore 54 lakh in remittance came to Bangladesh through banking channels in the first five days of April 2024, over BDT 4,950 crore at BDT 110 per dollar (the headline says USD 46 crore); about BDT 1,000 crore worth per day.

In the first five days of April 2024, remittance came through state-owned banks USD 3 crore 85 lakh, one specialised bank USD 2 crore 73 lakh, private banks USD 38 crore 78 lakh and foreign banks USD 17 lakh 60 thousand.
Each bank gives a different dollar rate and remittance fetches more than BDT 110 per dollar; every year expatriate Bangladeshis send more dollars at the end of Ramadan before Eid al-Fitr.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 199 crore 68 lakh in March 2024, lower than February 2024 (USD 216 crore 45 lakh) and lower than March 2023.

Calendar-year remittance to Bangladesh: USD 2,190 crore in 2023, USD 2,130 crore in 2022 (growth about 3 percent in 2023), USD 2,207 crore in 2021, USD 2,173 crore in 2020 and USD 1,833 crore in 2019. December 2023 was USD 198 crore 98 lakh and November 2023 USD 193 crore.

key_quote_bn: প্রতিবছর ঈদুল ফিতরের আগে রমজান মাসের শেষ দিকে স্বাভাবিক সময়ের তুলনায় প্রবাসী বাংলাদেশিরা বেশি বেশি ডলার পাঠান।

headline_en: Remittance fell before Eid
summary_en: Remittance to Bangladesh in March 2024 was USD 199 crore 68 lakh, lower than February 2024 and March 2023 even though Eid was approaching. The rate banks pay for remittance dollars had fallen from over BDT 120 to BDT 115-116 against an official BDT 110, and banks add their own 2.5 percent incentive to the government's 2.5 percent.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in March 2024 was USD 199 crore 68 lakh, lower than February 2024 (USD 216 crore 45 lakh) and lower than March 2023.

Calendar-year remittance to Bangladesh: USD 2,190 crore in 2023, USD 2,130 crore in 2022 (growth about 3 percent in 2023), USD 2,207 crore in 2021, USD 2,173 crore in 2020 and USD 1,833 crore in 2019. December 2023 was USD 198 crore 98 lakh and November 2023 USD 193 crore.

Mutual Trust Bank managing director Syed Mahbubur Rahman said the dollar price for remittance had fallen somewhat but had started rising again, that he could not understand why the expected pre-Eid remittance did not come, and that many may have sent in February or may send in April.
facts.source_in_article: Syed Mahbubur Rahman, managing director, Mutual Trust Bank

facts.statement: The official dollar price for buying remittance was BDT 110; because of the dollar crisis banks had been buying remittance at more than BDT 120 per dollar, and by about the end of March 2024 the rate had come down to BDT 115-116.
Bank officials think some people have brought back money laundered out of Bangladesh by showing it as remittance.

The Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers Association (BAFEDA) and the Association of Bankers Bangladesh (ABB), both bodies of commercial banks, have been setting the dollar exchange rate from time to time depending on supply and demand.
Banks in Bangladesh now give their own incentive on remittances equal to the government's 2.5 percent incentive (so 2.5 percent from government plus 2.5 percent from the bank).

named_actors.name: Syed Mahbubur Rahman
named_actors.what_the_article_says: Managing director of Mutual Trust Bank; commented on weak pre-Eid remittance

headline_en: USD 141 crore remittance came in the first three weeks of March
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 141 crore in remittances through banks in the first 22 days of March 2024. In the first eight months of fiscal year 2023-24 the UAE became the top source country, followed by the UK, Saudi Arabia, the USA and Italy, as legal-channel inflows from Saudi Arabia and the USA fell.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh through banks in the first 22 days of March 2024 was USD 141 crore: USD 51 crore on 1-8 March, USD 51 crore on 9-15 March and USD 40 crore on 16-22 March.

Of the USD 141 crore received up to 22 March 2024, USD 18 crore came through state-owned commercial banks and USD 120 crore through private commercial banks; among private banks Islami Bank brought the most, USD 40 crore.
Remittance in February 2024 was USD 217 crore (this article's figure), about 39 percent more than February 2023.
Eid al-Fitr in 2023 was in the third week of April; remittance in April 2023 was USD 168 crore and in March 2023 USD 202 crore.
Remittance to Bangladesh was USD 2,161 crore in fiscal year 2022-23 and USD 1,508 crore in the first eight months (July-February) of fiscal year 2023-24.

In the first eight months of fiscal year 2023-24 the most remittance to Bangladesh came from the United Arab Emirates, followed by the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, the United States and Italy. In the previous two fiscal years Saudi Arabia was first, the United States second, the UAE third and the UK fourth.

Banking-sector people say remittance through legal channels from Saudi Arabia and the United States has fallen while that from the UAE and the UK has risen, which explains the change in country ranking.
Banks in Bangladesh now give their own incentive on remittances equal to the government's 2.5 percent incentive (so 2.5 percent from government plus 2.5 percent from the bank).

key_quote_bn: চলতি অর্থবছরের প্রথম আট মাসে সৌদি আরব ও যুক্তরাষ্ট্রকে পেছনে ফেলে শীর্ষে উঠে এসেছে ইউএই ও যুক্তরাজ্য।

headline_en: Remittance up 39% in February
summary_en: Expatriates sent USD 216 crore 60 lakh to Bangladesh in February 2024, 38.77 percent more than February 2023 and more than January 2024. Banks were paying over BDT 120 per dollar for remittances against an official rate of BDT 110, plus a bank incentive matching the government's 2.5 percent.

facts.statement: Remittance to Bangladesh in February 2024 was USD 216 crore 60 lakh, against USD 210 crore in January 2024 and USD 156 crore 10 lakh in February 2023, a year-on-year rise of 38.77 percent.

Calendar-year remittance to Bangladesh: USD 2,190 crore in 2023, USD 2,130 crore in 2022 (growth about 3 percent in 2023), USD 2,207 crore in 2021, USD 2,173 crore in 2020 and USD 1,833 crore in 2019. December 2023 was USD 198 crore 98 lakh and November 2023 USD 193 crore.

The official dollar price for buying remittance was BDT 110, but because of the dollar crisis banks were buying remittance at more than BDT 120 per dollar, which is raising remittance through legal channels.
Bank officials think some people are bringing back money laundered out of Bangladesh by showing it as remittance.

The Bangladesh Foreign Exchange Dealers Association (BAFEDA) and the Association of Bankers Bangladesh (ABB), both bodies of commercial banks, have been setting the dollar exchange rate from time to time depending on supply and demand.
Banks in Bangladesh now give their own incentive on remittances equal to the government's 2.5 percent incentive (so 2.5 percent from government plus 2.5 percent from the bank).

key_quote_bn: ডলার-সংকটের কারণে ব্যাংকগুলো ডলারপ্রতি ১২০ টাকারও বেশি দামে প্রবাসী আয় কিনছে।
